Bee Foundation · Beekeeper survey · Winter 2025–2026

One in five colonies did not survive the winter.

What the survey links to higher losses

A plain-language walk through the 2025–2026 survey results. Each screen makes one point, shows the chart behind it, and explains how the number was calculated.

828
apiaries in the analysis
692
beekeepers who answered
4,843
colonies going into winter
1,047
colonies lost by spring

The headline

21.6% of colonies were lost over the winter.

Out of 4,843 colonies that went into winter, 1,047 were gone by spring. That is roughly one colony in five.

Losses were far from even. Some groups of beekeepers lost around one colony in ten, others lost two in five. The rest of this report looks at which answers in the survey go together with higher or lower losses.

How we calculated this

For each apiary: colonies lost = colonies in autumn 2025 minus colonies alive in spring 2026.

loss = total lost ÷ total in autumn = 1,047 ÷ 4,843 = 21.6%

We add up colonies across all apiaries first and then divide. So a beekeeper with 40 colonies counts more than one with 2. We call this the hive-weighted loss, and every percentage in this report is calculated this way.

Five survey rows were left out: one summary row without an apiary number and four apiaries with zero colonies in autumn.

Summary

What goes together with higher losses

  • Clear link

    Feeding only honey for winter

    40.5% lost, about double the 19.5% of beekeepers who fed honey plus sugar.

  • Clear link

    Treating varroa in only one season

    Winter-only 31.8% and summer-only 28.4% lost, against 13–19% with a full treatment.

  • Mostly explained by other factors

    Beekeeping method

    Natural beekeepers lost 26.9%, controlled 13.6%. Much of the gap reflects how they feed and treat.

  • Suggestive, small groups

    Honey only and no treatment together

    45.1% lost in this group of 62 apiaries. Full treatment seems to help honey feeders, but the evidence is not conclusive.

  • Clear link

    Few different crops around the apiary

    Each extra crop type within 1 km goes with about 9% lower odds of losing a colony.

  • Unexpected direction

    Pesticide exposure index

    Higher estimated exposure went with lower losses. We think the index mostly measures farmland, and we cannot separate the two.

These are associations in survey data from one winter. They show which groups lost more, not that one thing caused the other.

Finding 1 · Winter feed

Colonies fed only honey were lost twice as often.

40.5%lost with honey only (110 apiaries)
19.5%lost with honey + sugar (538 apiaries)

Feeding sugar only (20.3%) and honey plus sugar (19.5%) give almost the same result. The jump is in the honey-only group.

Honey-only feeders also tend to be natural beekeepers and often do not treat varroa. So we checked whether the gap survives when we compare beekeepers with the same method and the same varroa treatment. It does: the model still puts honey-only losses at 39.0% against 19.5%.

How we calculated this

Top chart: hive-weighted loss in each feed group, as on the headline screen.

Bottom chart: a statistical model (Model 3) that looks at feed, varroa treatment and method at the same time. The bars show the predicted loss if every apiary kept its own method and treatment and only its feed changed. The black tick is the observed loss.

odds ratio honey only vs honey + sugar = 2.71 (95% CI 1.61–4.59), p < 0.001

Finding 2 · Varroa treatment

Treating in only one season went with the highest losses.

31.8%lost with winter-only treatment
13.4%lost with an alternative full treatment

Beekeepers who treated in winter only (31.8%) or in summer only (28.4%) lost more colonies than those who did not treat at all (24.8%). Both full approaches did best: the classic 3-step treatment (19.1%) and an alternative full schedule (13.4%).

After accounting for feed and method, winter-only and summer-only treatment still stand out, with about 2.7 times the odds of loss compared with an alternative full treatment. The no-treatment group is not clearly different once feed and method are taken into account.

How we calculated this

Top chart: hive-weighted loss per treatment answer. The dashed line is the overall 21.6%.

Bottom chart: predicted loss from Model 3 with feed and method held the same.

winter only: OR 2.77 (1.57–4.87), p < 0.001
summer only: OR 2.62 (1.48–4.63), p < 0.001
no treatment: OR 1.74 (0.87–3.50), p = 0.12

Comparison group: alternative full treatment.

Finding 3 · Beekeeping method

Natural beekeepers lost twice as much, mostly because of how they feed and treat.

26.9%lost by natural beekeepers (96 apiaries)
13.6%lost by controlled beekeepers (86 apiaries)

Method and practice go together. Of the natural beekeepers, 57% feed only honey and 70% do not treat varroa. Among controlled beekeepers those shares are 3.5% and 5.8%.

When we compare beekeepers who feed and treat the same way, the predicted loss for natural beekeepers drops from 26.9% to 21.7%, and none of the method differences is statistically clear. The method label matters less than the feed and treatment choices behind it.

How we calculated this

Shares come from a cross-table of method against feed and treatment (results/02_method_x_*.csv).

Model 3, vs controlled:
natural OR 1.58 (0.65–3.83), p = 0.31
regular OR 1.76 (0.96–3.24), p = 0.07

Finding 4 · Feed and treatment together

Honey-only feeders who did a full 3-step treatment lost far fewer colonies.

45.1%honey only, no treatment (62 apiaries)
16.4%honey only, full 3-step (21 apiaries)

Each square shows the loss for one combination of treatment and feed. Green is lower loss, red is higher. The whole right-hand column (honey only) is warm, except the top square: honey feeders who did the full 3-step treatment lost no more than anyone else.

Read with care. Several squares hold fewer than 15 apiaries and are marked “too few”. The honey-only 3-step group has only 21 apiaries. When we test this comparison properly, allowing for the fact that we ran four tests, the result is borderline (p = 0.07). It is a promising lead, not a proven effect.

How we calculated this

Each square is the hive-weighted loss for apiaries with that feed and that treatment.

We decided in advance to test four specific comparisons with Model 4, which lets the effect of treatment differ by feed type. We then applied a Holm correction, which raises the bar for significance because we ran four tests.

honey only, none vs 3-step: OR 4.70, p = 0.018 → 0.068 after correction

All factors at once

Feed and partial treatment stand out when everything is weighed together.

This chart summarises Model 3. Each dot compares one group with a reference group: controlled method, honey + sugar feed, and alternative full varroa treatment.

A dot at 1 means the same odds of losing a colony as the reference group. A dot at 2 means double the odds. The line shows the range we are fairly confident about (95%). Red dots are lines that stay clear of 1.

Three dots are red: honey-only feed, winter-only treatment and summer-only treatment. All other lines cross 1, so for those groups we cannot rule out that they did no better or worse than the reference.

How we calculated this

A logistic model (GEE) fitted on every colony, where the outcome is whether the colony died. Apiaries of the same beekeeper are allowed to resemble each other, so a beekeeper with several apiaries does not count as independent evidence several times over.

825 apiaries with method, feed and treatment all answered.

Finding 5 · Landscape: crop diversity

Apiaries surrounded by more kinds of crops lost fewer colonies.

20.5%lost with 0–2 crop types within 1 km
10.9%lost with 9 or more crop types

The more different crops grow within 1 km, the lower the loss, step by step. This holds after accounting for feed, treatment and method: each extra crop type goes with about 9% lower odds of losing a colony.

Landscape data exist for 420 of the 828 apiaries. Their overall loss is 18.3%, a bit lower than the full survey.

How we calculated this

Crop diversity = number of crop types that cover more than 1% of the circle around the apiary and carry a pesticide factor above 0.

1 km: OR 0.91 per extra crop type (0.86–0.96), p = 0.001
500 m: OR 0.91 (0.84–0.98), p = 0.015

The groups in the chart (0–2, 3–5, 6–8, 9+) are only for display. The model uses the exact count.

Finding 6 · Landscape: pesticide exposure

A higher pesticide index went with lower losses. We do not think this means pesticides help.

25.2%lost where the index is zero
12.9%lost where the index is highest

The index is an estimate from land use, not a measurement of pesticide residues in hives. It is high where there is a lot of farmland with crops that are often sprayed. Crop diversity is high in exactly the same places: the two indices are strongly correlated (r = 0.70). With this data we cannot tell the two apart.

Among honey-only feeders (about 70 apiaries with landscape data) neither index shows a clear link. That group is too small for a firm answer.

How we calculated this

toxicity index = Σ (foraging factor × pesticide factor × % of circle covered)

Groups in the chart: zero, then the non-zero values split into three equal-sized groups.

1 km: OR 0.91 per index unit (0.85–0.98), p = 0.016
500 m: OR 0.93 (0.87–0.99), p = 0.031

One index unit is roughly a circle fully covered with maize.

Other survey questions

What beekeepers saw in their hives tells us less.

We also looked at three observation questions. They were not used in the models because an observation is often a result of a colony's condition, not a cause of it.

Deformed wings observed: no difference at all between answers (p = 0.92).

Varroa observed: beekeepers who observed no varroa lost the most (31.2%). We think this group partly includes beekeepers who did not check. We have not verified this.

Asian hornet observed: those who observed none lost slightly more (25.9%) than those who saw many (18.7%). This may reflect where hornets occur rather than any effect. We have not checked this either.

What this means

Three points for beekeepers

  1. Full cycle varroa treatment lowers mortality. Treating in only one season went with the highest losses, higher even than not treating. Both full-cycle approaches had the lowest losses.
  2. Be careful with honey-only winter feeding. Although this method is prefered by natural-based beekeepers, it also went with double the loss. Honey feeders who also did a full varroa treatment did much better, though that group is small.
  3. The surroundings matter too. Apiaries with more different crops nearby lost fewer colonies.
  4. Effects of pesticide require further research. The pesticide index result is unexplained and needs a better measure before drawing conclusions.

Limits of this survey

  • One winter of self-reported data. Patterns may differ next year.
  • Some groups are small, especially combinations with honey-only feed.
  • Landscape data exist for only 420 of 828 apiaries.
  • Due to the difficulty of accessing data, the toxicity index is estimated from land use, not measured.

Appendix · How the numbers were made

From survey answers to the charts in this report

  1. Cleaning (notebook 01). 833 survey rows. One summary row without an apiary number and four apiaries with zero colonies in autumn removed. 828 apiaries remain. Only coded answers are kept; no names, addresses or coordinates.
  2. Losses. Lost = colonies in autumn 2025 minus colonies alive in spring 2026. Percentages are hive-weighted: total lost divided by total in autumn, per group.
  3. Group differences (notebook 02). Chi-square tests per question, then pairwise tests with a Bonferroni correction.
  4. Models (notebook 03). Logistic GEE on colony level, grouped by beekeeper. Model 1: feed and treatment. Model 3: adds method. Model 4: adds feed × treatment combinations, used for four pre-planned comparisons with Holm correction. As a check, we repeated the models with each apiary counted equally. Honey-only feed and summer-only treatment stay significant; winter-only treatment becomes weaker (p = 0.25) and no treatment becomes significant (OR 2.22). Small apiaries weigh more in that version, which shifts the treatment results.
  5. Landscape (notebooks 04 and 05). Land use within 500 m and 1 km of 423 apiaries. Toxicity and crop diversity indices per apiary, then the same GEE set-up with feed, treatment and method as controls.

Code and result tables: github.com/Nora-Dongdong/bee-mortality-survey, branch rewrite-2025-2026. OR = odds ratio; CI = 95% confidence interval.
